questions.stem: A developer joins a repository that has no `.claude/` directory. Which command produces a first-pass `CLAUDE.md` by analysing the codebase?

options.text: `/init`
`/memory`
`/config`
`/bootstrap`

questions.explanation: `/init` inspects the project — build tooling, test commands, layout, conventions — and writes a starter `CLAUDE.md`. `/memory` opens existing memory files for editing; `/config` opens settings; `/bootstrap` does not exist.

distractor_notes.B: Edits memory files that already exist; it does not generate one from the codebase.

analogy.text: `/init` is `npm init` or `terraform init` — it produces the scaffold you then curate by hand.

questions.stem: What is the intended purpose of `.claude/settings.local.json`, and how should it be handled in version control?

options.text: Machine-specific overrides for one developer; it should be git-ignored.
The canonical team configuration; it should be committed and reviewed.
A cache Claude Code regenerates; it can be deleted safely at any time and never edited.
Enterprise policy applied to the local machine; only administrators may edit it.

questions.explanation: `settings.local.json` sits above `settings.json` in precedence and exists for personal overrides — an extra allowed tool, a different model while experimenting. Because it is personal, it belongs in `.gitignore`; the shared truth stays in `settings.json`.

distractor_notes.D: Enterprise policy lives in the managed-settings path outside the repository.

questions.stem: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe plan mode.

options.text: It restricts the session to read-only analysis until the user approves a plan.
It automatically applies the plan once the model finishes writing it.
It can be entered by cycling permission modes with Shift+Tab.
It disables the Read and Grep tools to save context.
It requires a `plan` block in `CLAUDE.md` to be available.

questions.explanation: Plan mode is a read-only permission mode: the agent investigates and proposes, and nothing is mutated until the human accepts. Shift+Tab cycles through the permission modes in the interactive UI.

distractor_notes.B: Approval is the entire point — auto-apply would defeat it.
distractor_notes.D: Reading is exactly what plan mode is for.

analogy.text: `terraform plan` versus `terraform apply`. Plan mode is the dry run you read before you let anything change.

questions.stem: A team lead wants to know how much the current session has cost so far, without leaving the session. Which command reports it?

options.text: `/context`
`/cost`
`/status`
`/usage`

questions.explanation: `/cost` reports token usage and spend for the session. `/context` shows how the context window is being consumed, which is a related but different question — one is money, the other is room.

distractor_notes.D: Not the cost command in Claude Code.

questions.stem: An engineer keeps one Claude Code session open all week across unrelated tickets. Quality drops and cost per turn climbs. What is the root cause and the correct remedy?

options.text: The model degrades over time; restart the CLI daily.
Accumulated irrelevant context dilutes attention and inflates every request; start a fresh session per task and use `/clear` at task boundaries.
Token pricing rises with session age; open a new billing session each morning.
The context window shrinks as it fills; enlarge it in settings.

questions.explanation: Every prior turn is re-sent as input on each request, so a long, topic-mixed transcript costs more per turn *and* competes for the model's attention with the task actually at hand. Task-scoped sessions are the single highest-leverage habit for both quality and spend.

distractor_notes.A: Nothing about the model changes; the input does.
distractor_notes.C: Pricing is per token, not per session age.
distractor_notes.D: The window is fixed; it is being consumed, not shrinking.

analogy.text: It is the same discipline as short-lived feature branches. A branch you keep rebasing for three weeks accumulates conflict surface; so does a session.

questions.stem: Which environment variable routes Claude Code inference through Google Vertex AI?

options.text: `ANTHROPIC_VERTEX=true`
`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1`
`GOOGLE_CLOUD_CLAUDE=enabled`
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=vertex`

questions.explanation: `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1` selects Vertex AI, mirroring `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` for Amazon Bedrock. Region and project are then supplied through the usual Google Cloud variables.

distractor_notes.D: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at a gateway URL, not a provider keyword.

questions.stem: Inside an interactive session, what does typing `@src/auth/session.ts` in a prompt do?

options.text: Nothing special; it is treated as literal text.
It references that file so its contents are pulled into context for the turn.
It opens the file in the user's editor.
It permanently pins the file into every future turn of the session.

questions.explanation: `@` is the file-reference affordance: it brings the named file (or directory listing) into context for the request, which is far cheaper and more precise than asking the agent to search for it.

distractor_notes.C: It does not drive the editor.
distractor_notes.D: It affects the turn, not a permanent pin.

analogy.text: It is the difference between saying 'look at the auth code somewhere' and pasting the exact file link into the review comment.

questions.stem: Which permission rule allows the test suite to be run but does NOT allow arbitrary npm scripts?

options.text: `Bash(npm:*)`
`Bash(npm run test:*)`
`Bash`
`Bash(*test*)`

questions.explanation: Rules are `Tool(specifier)` and the specifier is prefix-matched with `:*` acting as the wildcard tail. `Bash(npm run test:*)` matches `npm run test`, `npm run test:unit`, `npm run test -- --watch`, and nothing else. `Bash(npm:*)` would also permit `npm publish`.

distractor_notes.A: Far too broad — includes publish, install, arbitrary scripts.
distractor_notes.D: Not the rule syntax; leading wildcards are not how specifiers match.

questions.stem: A security team wants database migrations to always require a human decision, and wants production credential files to be unreachable entirely. How should the rules be expressed?

options.text: Both in `deny`, since deny is the strongest control.
Migrations in `ask`, credential files in `deny`.
Both in `ask`, so an engineer can always override in an emergency.
Migrations in `allow` with a PostToolUse hook, credential files in `ask`.

questions.explanation: `ask` forces an explicit human confirmation each time — right for an operation that is legitimate but consequential. `deny` refuses outright with no prompt — right for something that should never happen, where even offering the prompt is a social-engineering surface.

distractor_notes.A: Denying migrations blocks legitimate work and pushes engineers outside the tool.
distractor_notes.C: A prompt on credential reads is exactly the moment a prompt-injection payload wants a tired human to click Allow.
distractor_notes.D: A PostToolUse hook fires after the migration has already run.

analogy.text: `ask` is a manual approval action before the deploy stage. `deny` is an SCP that makes the API call impossible — no prompt, no human in the loop to fool.

questions.stem: A CI workflow needs a second headless step to continue the exact conversation started by an earlier step. What must the first step capture, and how is it used?

options.text: The PID of the first process, passed to `--attach`.
The `session_id` from the JSON output, passed to `--resume <id> -p`.
Nothing; `--continue` always finds the right session in CI.
The full transcript, re-supplied as the next prompt.

questions.explanation: JSON output carries a `session_id`. Passing it to `--resume <id>` together with `-p` continues that specific conversation non-interactively — the standard pattern for multi-stage pipelines.

distractor_notes.A: Sessions are not attached by PID.
distractor_notes.C: `--continue` depends on 'most recent for this directory', which is fragile when runners are ephemeral or parallel.
distractor_notes.D: Wasteful and lossy; the session already holds it.

snippet.title: Two-stage headless pipeline
snippet.code:
# Stage 1 — analyse
out=$(claude -p "Analyse the failing tests" --output-format json)
sid=$(echo "$out" | jq -r '.session_id')

# Stage 2 — act, in the same conversation
claude --resume "$sid" -p "Now propose the minimal fix" --output-format json

options.text: In `CLAUDE.md`, as a fenced `hooks` block.
In `settings.json` under a `hooks` key, editable through `/hooks`.
In `.claude/hooks/*.sh`, discovered by filename convention only.
In `.mcp.json`, alongside server definitions.

questions.explanation: Hooks are configuration, not instructions: they live in the `hooks` key of the settings files and follow the same precedence chain. The `/hooks` command gives an interactive editor over that configuration. Scripts may live anywhere; the matcher and command are what get registered.

distractor_notes.A: `CLAUDE.md` is prompt context, not executable configuration.
distractor_notes.D: That file is for MCP servers.

questions.stem: A `--dangerously-skip-permissions` run is being proposed for an autonomous refactoring job. Select the TWO conditions that make this defensible.

options.text: The job runs in a disposable container with no network egress and no production credentials.
The engineer promises to watch the terminal.
The working tree is a throwaway clone whose only output is a pull request a human reviews.
The repository has a comprehensive `CLAUDE.md`.
The model is set to the most capable tier available.

questions.explanation: Skipping permissions removes the interactive guardrail, so the guardrail has to be reconstructed from the environment: blast radius bounded by isolation, and a human review gate on the way out. Neither vigilance, documentation quality, nor model capability constrains what a tool call can reach.

distractor_notes.B: Attention is not a control; the prompts you removed were the control.
distractor_notes.D: Good context improves behaviour but grants no containment.
distractor_notes.E: A more capable model still executes whatever it decides to execute.

analogy.text: It is running a pod as privileged. Sometimes justified — but only on a node pool you are willing to lose, never on the cluster holding production secrets.
